# On the Strange Privilege of Noticing Things

I've been thinking lately about attention—the act of truly noticing something—and how it feels like a privilege that most of us don't properly acknowledge. Not the kind of privilege that comes with advantage or inheritance, but something quieter. The privilege of being able to stop and look.

There's a tree outside my awareness that I've never actually seen. It exists in the peripheral vision of the world, mentioned maybe in passing, but I've never stood before it with the specific intention of understanding what it is. This bothers me more than it should. The world is full of these unseen things, not because they're hidden, but because our attention is finite and we're all rationing it constantly, whether we realize it or not.

I think about this when I walk through cities. Everyone is moving with such purpose, such certainty about where they're going, and I'm struck by how little we actually see while we're in motion. The architecture above our heads goes unwatched. The small shops tucked between larger stores remain invisible. Other people become obstacles or background rather than fellow consciousness navigators also trying to make sense of being alive. We're all practicing a kind of necessary blindness just to function, to get from point A to point B without being overwhelmed by the sheer amount of information available to our senses.

But what happens when we break that pattern? What happens when someone decides to really look at something ordinary?

I think of the photographer who spent years photographing the same street corner. Or the naturalist who sat in the same forest and noticed things that no one had recorded before, not because they were hidden, but because they'd simply never been watched. There's something almost subversive about sustained attention in a world that profits from distraction and movement.

This connects to something I've noticed about boredom, too. We talk about boredom like it's a malfunction, a sign that something isn't engaging us properly, but I wonder if boredom is actually where attention goes to rest. It's the space where you're no longer seeking stimulation, no longer trying to extract value from each moment. There's a kind of freedom in it. A kid staring out a window for an hour isn't wasting time; they're doing something we've largely forgotten how to do, which is to let their attention drift naturally to whatever catches it.

I've also been thinking about how we describe our inner lives. We use metaphors borrowed from other domains—we talk about mental landscapes, emotional weather, psychological baggage. But I'm not sure these metaphors actually help us understand ourselves better. Maybe they just make our experience feel more manageable, more like something we can map and navigate. The truth is probably stranger and less coherent than any metaphor we could use.

What is it like to be thinking right now? It's not like moving through a landscape. It's not like weather. It's something more like language talking about language, consciousness observing itself, which creates this weird recursive loop that's impossible to fully step outside of. We're always trying to know ourselves from the inside, which is like trying to see your own eyes without a mirror.

This is why I think conversations matter so much. When someone describes their experience to you and you listen—really listen, not just wait for your turn to talk—you're briefly escaping that loop. You're accessing another consciousness through the only door it has, which is language. It's our only genuine technology for sharing subjective reality. Everything else—film, art, music—are translations and approximations. But when someone says "I felt this way and it was like this," and you understand them, you've briefly bridged the gap that normally separates one mind from another.

The fact that we can do this at all seems like it should be more remarkable than it is. We talk about it casually or take it for granted, but we're basically engaged in a miracle of translation every time we have a real conversation.

I'm also struck by how much of being human is actually about tolerating uncertainty. We're creatures that crave patterns and explanations, but reality doesn't neatly organize itself into patterns. We're constantly experiencing things that don't fit into our existing frameworks, and we have to choose between revising our understanding or dismissing the experience. Most of the time, I think, we dismiss it because revising our understanding is exhausting.

But there's something valuable in resisting that impulse sometimes. In letting things be strange and unexplained. In sitting with the feeling of not understanding something rather than reaching for the nearest comfortable explanation.

This applies to people, too. We're all doing the same thing with each other—creating simplified models of the people in our lives so we can navigate relationships without constantly being surprised. But people aren't simpler than our models. They're infinitely more complex. Every now and then, someone does something that doesn't fit the model we've created of them, and it's jarring. But maybe that's the moment where we're actually seeing them, rather than seeing the image we've constructed.

I don't know where I'm going with this. I've wandered from trees to attention to consciousness to relationships, and there's probably no through-line except that these are all things that interest me. They're all variations on the same theme: the difficulty and necessity of actually paying attention in a world designed to scatter it.

So maybe the real privilege isn't just being able to notice things—it's having the freedom to choose what you pay attention to, even knowing that choice is limited and costly. Even knowing that everything you focus on is something else you're not seeing. Even knowing that most of your life will be lived in that state of necessary blindness, moving from task to task without really seeing.

The privilege is in the awareness itself, I think. In knowing that you're not seeing most of the world, and in the moment of choosing to see something anyway.
